source_text: Nam si ante legem non imputata est peccati tradux, post legem autem non fuit, numquam omnino, quo noceret humano generi, virus obtinuit. Ante legem enim imputatum non est naturale peccatum, sub lege imputatum non est, quia in nullo umquam loco legis vel monstratum hoc vel imputatum docetur. Apparet ergo Apostolum peccatum ante legem liberae voluntatis, post legem autem praevaricationem totidem liberae voluntatis arguere.
pass_a_gloss: For if before the law the tradux of sin was not imputed, but after the law it was not, never altogether did a poison obtain by which it would harm the human race. For before the law a natural sin was not imputed, under the law it was not imputed, because in no place of the law ever is this taught as either shown or imputed. It appears therefore that the Apostle accuses a sin of free will before the law, but after the law a transgression of equally free will.

lemmas.lexica: LS praevaricatio; Blaise Adam's transgression as example
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: For if sin transmitted by descent was not imputed before the law, and did not exist after the law, it never possessed any poison capable of harming the human race. Natural sin was not imputed before the law; it was not imputed under the law either, since nowhere in the law is it ever shown to have been revealed or imputed. Plainly, then, the apostle accuses sin committed by free will before the law, and transgression likewise committed by free will after the law (compare Romans 5:13).

choices.why: Adam's act of crossing the command; Julian's example of sin, not a transmitted nature.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
